# UI/UX design: inclusive systems
Source: https://llmsx.org/tree/ui-ux-design-inclusive-systems/

# UI/UX design: inclusive systems — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for UI/UX design: inclusive systems. Run status: COMPLETED.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.4.1 · generated 2026-11-09 · budgeted to ≈8000 tokens; the full catalogue is llms-full.txt -->

## Structure and components

- [statement] GOV.UK’s contribution criteria make inclusive evidence part of publication readiness: components must work in research with a representative sample including users with disabilities, and across browsers, assistive technologies and devices. The criteria also require clarity about the contexts actually tested. (low confidence) — https://design-system.service.gov.uk/community/contribution-criteria/
- [statement] Preply’s practitioner account distinguishes coverage (usage) from adoption (correct usage). It also tracks documentation, platform parity and user feedback, so a usage increase alone should not be reported as proof of correct component use or system quality. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/preply-engineering/visual-coverage-why-and-how-preply-measures-the-impact-of-the-design-system-1057115f4aff
- [statement] UXPin recommends explicit approval rights for components, variants, breaking changes and exceptions, plus a logged exception path with an expiry date or migration plan. (low confidence) — https://www.uxpin.com/studio/blog/design-system-governance/
- [statement] UXPin describes a component lifecycle from proposal through review, build, documentation, release, adoption measurement and deprecation; it asks for use-case and reuse evidence before adding variants. (low confidence) — https://www.uxpin.com/studio/blog/design-system-governance/
- [statement] In Curtis’s spec-driven approach, component specifications describe the public API, variant rules and composed examples; supplemental requirements capture behavior, accessibility and state precedence such as `disabled` over `read-only`. (low confidence) — https://nathanacurtis.substack.com/p/spec-driven-ui-component-development
- [statement] Communicate component retirement before removal: GOV.UK describes deprecation as advance notice of a future breaking change, while zeroheight warns that deleting an in-use component immediately can leave gaps and lost references. (medium confidence) — https://frontend.design-system.service.gov.uk/v5/staying-up-to-date/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://help.zeroheight.com/hc/en-us/articles/36474257606555-Deprecating-in-design-systems-When-it-s-time-to-say-goodbye
- [statement] zeroheight recommends inspecting component dependencies and replacement fit before retirement: check direct template usage, nesting in larger components, whether replacements differ by use case, and whether contained components also become redundant. (low confidence) — https://help.zeroheight.com/hc/en-us/articles/36474257606555-Deprecating-in-design-systems-When-it-s-time-to-say-goodbye
- [statement] Preply explicitly avoids mandatory visual-coverage targets: bespoke needs and third-party components can justify lower coverage. Its account also warns that popular public pages can obscure other teams in aggregate measurements. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/preply-engineering/visual-coverage-why-and-how-preply-measures-the-impact-of-the-design-system-1057115f4aff
- [statement] A composite token contains named subvalues for related styling properties applied together; it is not merely an arbitrary group of independently organized tokens. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/
- [statement] Resolve aliases after context selection and ordered overrides have produced the final token structure. The resolver allows deep alias chains but forbids circular references and requires the referenced type to match. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/
- [statement] DTCG composite tokens combine multiple named sub-values in a predefined structure. Tokens Studio distinguishes these from its legacy generic composition token, which its guide recommends replacing with independently defined token types. (high confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://docs.tokens.studio/manage-tokens/token-types/composition
- [statement] Resolver ordering is significant: later sets or selected modifier contexts override earlier conflicting tokens. Aliases must resolve after the ordered token structure has been flattened. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/
- [statement] Handoff specifications should make states and responsive behavior explicit. The developers interviewed by zeroheight describe missing intermediate-width behavior, long-content rules, and empty states; Figma’s guide describes component documentation that includes variants and states. (medium confidence) — https://zeroheight.com/blog/what-do-developers-want-in-a-design-handoff-we-asked-them/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://www.figma.com/best-practices/guide-to-developer-handoff/
- [statement] Plan accessible venues or remote participation, transportation, breaks and usable materials as part of recruitment logistics; budget participant payments and access-related expenses. (medium confidence) — https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] W3C recommends tightly wrapping each opposite-direction inline phrase, setting its base direction, and preserving nested directional structure. Directional isolation prevents the phrase from influencing surrounding text; unknown-direction content needs automatic direction determination and isolation. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/International/articles/inline-bidi-markup/
- [statement] Figma distinguishes user flows, which map user actions and decisions, from task flows focused on a single action and wireframes focused on interface layout and structure. These artifacts answer different design questions. (low confidence) — https://www.figma.com/resource-library/user-flow/
- [statement] A wireframe can make screen structure and layout testable without finished visual details. It should not be interpreted as evidence about every visual attribute of a finished interface. (medium confidence) — https://www.figma.com/resource-library/user-flow/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-prototype-hi-lo-fidelity/

## How it works

- [statement] Reduce memory demands by making process position and instructions visible: COGA recommends showing completed, current and pending steps, while Coforma recommends persistent instructions throughout multi-step processes. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://coforma.io/perspectives/give-users-brains-a-break-ux-tips-for-cognitive-accessibility?utm_source=title2info&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=07142025&utm_content=editorial
- [statement] COGA recommends authentication alternatives that do not require memorizing strings, calculations, copying content, puzzles, reproducing gestures, or transcribing displayed characters; these are design recommendations, not a claim that every authentication mechanism must have identical cognitive demands. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] COGA recommends avoiding timeouts and letting users save work as they go. If that is impossible, explain the available time and whether a timeout will discard entered data when the process begins. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] GOV.UK Frontend v5 guidance uses patch increments for bug fixes, minor increments for new features and major increments for potentially required consumer changes; it still directs consumers to read release notes and test upgrades because breaking impact depends on usage. (low confidence) — https://frontend.design-system.service.gov.uk/v5/staying-up-to-date/
- [statement] GOV.UK publication criteria require evidence from a representative sample including users with disabilities; limited deployment is acceptable when tested contexts are stated and wider feedback is encouraged. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08) — https://design-system.service.gov.uk/community/contribution-criteria/
- [statement] Cross-platform conversion can lose responsive typography behavior: the DTCG dimension definition permits a lossy fixed-size conversion when a target platform has no equivalent to relative root-font sizing. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/
- [statement] Mila Cann argues against discrete handoffs in agile teams because they imply design is finished; Cegid instead uses handoff to mean a transition into shared implementation responsibility. These are explicitly attributed process framings, not evidence that implementation documentation should be eliminated. (medium confidence) — https://medium.com/design-bootcamp/design-handoffs-dont-belong-in-agile-environments-61abba8e7848 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://composedesign.ila.cegid.com/blog/bridging-the-gap-collaboration-between-designer-and-developers-after-handoff/
- [statement] Make implementation-ready work distinguishable from drafts and experiments. Figma describes separating work by readiness; zeroheight records developer difficulty identifying the authoritative design among experiments. (medium confidence) — https://www.figma.com/best-practices/guide-to-developer-handoff/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://zeroheight.com/blog/what-do-developers-want-in-a-design-handoff-we-asked-them/
- [statement] Keep designers and developers engaged during delivery. Cegid recommends resolving implementation edge cases together; Figma describes early, frequent sharing as a way to obtain feedback before the end of the process. These are practitioner recommendations, not quantified causal estimates. (medium confidence) — https://composedesign.ila.cegid.com/blog/bridging-the-gap-collaboration-between-designer-and-developers-after-handoff/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://www.figma.com/best-practices/guide-to-developer-handoff/
- [statement] Modeinspect recommends actionable QA findings that record location, expected value, observed value, severity, and a screenshot. When an engineer fixes a finding through a comment or ticket, its workflow includes a second designer review of the updated build. (low confidence) — https://modeinspect.com/blog/design-qa
- [statement] Disability advocacy groups, community organizations and specialist accessibility panels provide recruitment channels. When using an agency, check its disability recruitment experience and specify the actual access needs relevant to the study. (medium confidence) — https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://tetralogical.com/blog/2022/08/01/inclusive-user-research-recruiting-participants/
- [statement] Treat consent as continuing: remind participants that participation is voluntary and check again when they appear uncomfortable or confused; allow withdrawal without forfeiting the promised incentive. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Explain any practical cutoff for withdrawing already anonymised or published data. Cambridge’s Inclusive Design Toolkit specifically advises disclosing when later withdrawal becomes impossible. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Offer consent materials in usable formats and provide a documented verbal-consent route when appropriate; a handwritten signature is not the only way these guides describe recording consent. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Explain that participation is voluntary and withdrawal is permitted; GOV.UK additionally advises checking continued consent when a participant seems uncomfortable or confused. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] The guides scope post-session withdrawal differently: GOV.UK prescribes deletion on withdrawal, while Cambridge explicitly addresses limits after anonymisation or repository publication. Treat these as attributed guidance and explain the study-specific withdrawal process and limits in advance. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Treat text alignment and text direction as separate design decisions. Material Design distinguishes the placement of a text box from the flow within it and identifies text entry, cursor position, punctuation, phone numbers and URLs as common RTL rendering trouble spots. (low confidence) — https://m3.material.io/foundations/layout/bidirectionality-rtl
- [statement] Do not reverse the digits inside a number when adapting an interface to RTL. Numeral shapes can still vary by locale; number localization and digit-order reversal are separate decisions. (medium confidence) — https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/right-to-left · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://m2.material.io/design/usability/bidirectionality.html

## How-to and procedures

- [statement] Use clear, concrete language and examples; keep content concise without losing precision. Both COGA and the AASPIRE guidelines recommend this approach. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6485264/
- [statement] Use COGA alongside WCAG to address cognitive usability needs beyond conformance; W3C explicitly describes COGA patterns as supplemental guidance, and DWP recommends cross-referencing them when improving services beyond AA. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://dwpdigital.blog.gov.uk/2022/06/30/designing-accessible-services-dont-exclude-the-neurodiverse/
- [statement] Use data within the consent obtained, minimize personal data collection, protect stored data and explain sharing and recordings to participants. (medium confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research
- [statement] Check locale-specific date formats, currency placement, decimal and grouping separators, measurement units, address forms and phone validation. SimpleLocalize lists these as localization QA checks. (low confidence) — https://simplelocalize.io/blog/posts/ui-localization-best-practices/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Limit interruptions and distracting motion, and provide user controls: COGA recommends control over interruptions and content changes, and AASPIRE recommends avoiding moving images and decorative visual or sonic clutter. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6485264/
- [statement] Fable cautions that automated checks cannot determine whether language is confusing, steps feel overwhelming or navigation is predictable; its article recommends validation by people with lived cognitive-accessibility experience. (low confidence) — https://makeitfable.com/article/cognitive-accessibility-pilot-case-study/
- [statement] DWP cautions against treating blanket AAA conformance as a universal solution, noting that some content cannot satisfy every AAA criterion; its recommended approach is to consider useful AAA criteria and cross-reference COGA patterns and user stories. (low confidence) — https://dwpdigital.blog.gov.uk/2022/06/30/designing-accessible-services-dont-exclude-the-neurodiverse/
- [statement] Matan Rosen recommends component specifications that enumerate states and variants, anatomy, boundaries, empty and error states, text constraints and keyboard interactions. This makes behavior and limits explicit alongside appearance. (low confidence) — https://uxdesign.cc/component-spec-the-design-system-component-delivery-5f88db6ccf7e
- [statement] Capozzi’s migration account identifies a coordination failure mode: automatic replacement leaves special cases that require consuming teams’ knowledge and roadmap capacity. Its numerical automation estimates are the author’s guesses, so they should not become general migration benchmarks. (low confidence) — https://maecapozzi.com/newsletter/75
- [statement] Resolver portability has a boundary: same-document references are mandatory, but tools may decline local-file or remote-URI imports. Bundling through optional definitions can also fail to transfer across tools that ignore those definitions. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/
- [statement] In Weblate issue 5340, a maintainer attributed an apparent Arabic punctuation displacement to stored character order and rendering context, and advised checking the consuming application. This historical support exchange illustrates why a JSON preview alone cannot establish correct bidi behavior. (low confidence) — https://github.com/WeblateOrg/weblate/issues/5340
- [statement] Test contraction as well as expansion, and inspect long unbreakable compounds. W3C notes that smaller translations can leave problematic whitespace and that compound words can fail to wrap where an English phrase wraps. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/International/articles/article-text-size/
- [statement] Do not generalize one disabled participant’s input to everyone. W3C warns that experience varies even within one disability; user involvement must be combined with accessibility standards and conformance evaluation because participants cannot cover all disabilities and assistive-technology configurations. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/WAI/planning/involving-users/
- [statement] In a UX Stack Exchange practitioner account, leaving error states and secondary screens until high-fidelity prototyping led to missing screens and user dead ends. The author later reported that covering error flows in wireframes saved team effort; this is an experience report, not a measured universal effect. (low confidence) — https://ux.stackexchange.com/questions/137052/should-i-cover-every-single-user-flow-including-error-states-in-wireframes-for-w
- [statement] Walker, Takayama and Landay found few differences in the number, type and severity of usability issues across paper/computer and low/high-fidelity website prototypes in their experiment. MeasuringU’s review likewise supports low-fidelity prototypes for finding major issues, while warning they are imperfect substitutes. This supports early issue discovery, not equivalence for every test outcome. (medium confidence) — https://www.leilatakayama.org/downloads/Takayama.Prototypes_HFES2002_prepress.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://measuringu.com/prototype-fidelity/
- [statement] GOV.UK warns that an online alpha prototype cannot support the full range of technical accessibility tests used for production code. Prototype findings therefore leave a specific validation boundary for the later implementation. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-alpha-phase-works

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] To support task preparation and planning, COGA recommends stating the expected effort, required resources and process overview before a multi-step task, and making in-progress versus completed status clear. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] Provide presentation choices rather than assume one display suits everyone: COGA recommends font, spacing and contrast preferences, and AASPIRE recommends color-palette choices and both smaller and larger fonts. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6485264/
- [statement] AASPIRE developed its guidelines through iterative autistic end-user involvement and empirically evaluated the resulting website; this is evidence about that intervention rather than proof that every recommendation works for every neurodivergent user. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6485264/
- [statement] In Fable’s pilot, some participants needed to complete tasks silently before explaining their thoughts, so its authors recommend offering a do-first option rather than requiring concurrent think-aloud; this is a pilot-specific observation, not a general incapacity attributed to neurodivergent users. (low confidence) — https://makeitfable.com/article/cognitive-accessibility-pilot-case-study/
- [statement] Design around functional needs rather than assuming a diagnosis determines a person’s interface needs. Fable recommends a needs-based approach, including people without formal diagnoses; W3C identifies memory, attention, processing, language, and learning barriers as distinct design concerns. (medium confidence) — https://makeitfable.com/article/cognitive-accessibility-pilot-case-study/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] Société Générale’s practitioner account describes a council that checks consistency, reviews documentation and supports contributions. Council membership depends on available time and enthusiasm; this is a contextual operating model rather than evidence that one structure fits every organization. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/societe-generale-design/taming-design-system-chaos-66bcadbf43e1
- [statement] Nathan Curtis argues that federation should augment dedicated central capacity rather than replace it. His practitioner account describes a stalled system after the responsible team was disbanded without relieving federated contributors of their existing responsibilities; it is not a controlled comparison of governance models. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/@nathanacurtis/the-fallacy-of-federated-design-systems-23b9a9a05542
- [statement] Deprecation should include a transition plan and visibility into consumption rather than immediate deletion. Zeroheight recommends communication and usage analysis; Mae Capozzi describes replacement parity, preventing new deprecated uses, automation and product-team help for cases requiring manual migration. (medium confidence) — https://help.zeroheight.com/hc/en-us/articles/36474257606555-Deprecating-in-design-systems-When-it-s-time-to-say-goodbye · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://maecapozzi.com/newsletter/75
- [statement] Preply describes visual coverage as a measure of design-system usage in rendered products, complementing static code analysis. Its account says coverage is one metric among several and is a diagnostic signal rather than a score teams must maximize. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/preply-engineering/visual-coverage-why-and-how-preply-measures-the-impact-of-the-design-system-1057115f4aff
- [statement] Preply distinguishes codebase usage from what users actually encounter; its visual coverage measures use of design-system components in products, rather than proving correct usage. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/preply-engineering/visual-coverage-why-and-how-preply-measures-the-impact-of-the-design-system-1057115f4aff
- [statement] UXPin presents governance structure as a tradeoff: a small or overloaded central team can bottleneck contributions, while federated contributions require communication and coordination and may introduce inconsistency when guidelines are not followed. (low confidence) — https://www.uxpin.com/studio/blog/design-system-governance/
- [statement] DTCG defines a platform-agnostic interchange format for design decisions; its purpose is to reduce bespoke integrations between design and development tools, rather than prescribe a particular authoring tool. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/
- [statement] Contentful distinguishes modes as variations within token collections and defines a theme, in its own model, as a separate complete token set retaining the same structure. Treat this as an attributed convention rather than a universal definition of themes. (low confidence) — https://www.contentful.com/blog/design-token-system/
- [statement] Tokens Studio documents a concrete composition limit: applying a composition token styles one layer rather than all child layers, and individual property tokens attached to Figma styles or variables do not appear as such in the Figma UI. (low confidence) — https://docs.tokens.studio/manage-tokens/token-types/composition
- [statement] Contentful uses mode for contextual value variations, collection for tokens that share modes, and theme for the full set of collections; the article cautions that theme is also sometimes used to mean mode. These are the article’s working definitions rather than universal interchange terminology. (low confidence) — https://www.contentful.com/blog/design-token-system/
- [statement] GDS recommends accessibility acceptance criteria that are specific, testable, and expressed as outcomes rather than prescribed solutions. In its method, criteria preserve earlier accessibility decisions and evolve when implementation or testing reveals missing needs. (low confidence) — https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2018/01/24/improving-accessibility-with-accessibility-acceptance-criteria/
- [statement] GOV.UK explicitly cautions that accessibility acceptance criteria alone do not make a service accessible; use them to preserve accessibility decisions across iterations rather than treating a completed checklist as sufficient assurance. (low confidence) — https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2018/01/24/improving-accessibility-with-accessibility-acceptance-criteria/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] W3C COGA Content Usable provides supplemental guidance beyond WCAG requirements; following it is not required for WCAG conformance. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] COGA recommends placing clear, concise instructions before or beside the activity, breaking them into complete steps, and supplying examples or illustrations. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] COGA recommends reducing unnecessary decisions and steps: keep required workflows to their minimally necessary steps and separate optional actions, to reduce distractions, mistakes, and mental fatigue. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] COGA recommends that context, functionality and settings changes be user initiated or have an easy off switch, together with an easy way to return to the previous state. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] Scope AASPIRE findings to their study context: the authors identify a simple informational website, a convenience evaluation sample, and primarily non-Hispanic white participants as limits. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6485264/
- [statement] COGA recommends making the page purpose and position within a task recognizable, including after a user loses focus. Its user stories explicitly connect these orientation needs with attention, memory, and executive-function impairments. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] COGA recommends an easy way to control interruptions, reminders, and changing content, except user-initiated events or emergencies; it describes pause controls and user-selected interruption settings as attention and memory supports. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] COGA recommends supporting personalization and simplification without disabling add-ons or extensions, including spelling support, password support, text-to-speech, and synchronized highlighting. It also recommends user-initiated context changes or an easy off switch, plus a way back to the previous context. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] Contribution governance can separate proposal eligibility from publication readiness: GOV.UK checks usefulness and uniqueness before reviewing usability, consistency and versatility; Société Générale describes a single request entry point with council triage and explicit outcomes. (medium confidence) — https://design-system.service.gov.uk/community/contribution-criteria/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://medium.com/societe-generale-design/taming-design-system-chaos-66bcadbf43e1
- [statement] GOV.UK Frontend v5 documents deprecation as advance notice of a future breaking change, usually in the next major version. Addressing deprecations incrementally reduces the work needed for a later major upgrade. (low confidence) — https://frontend.design-system.service.gov.uk/v5/staying-up-to-date/
- [statement] GOV.UK’s August 2026 research on prototype lifecycle labels found that “Trial” was broadly understood, while “Needs review” created uncertainty about onward use. Participants wanted context about accessibility testing and future changes. The findings support explaining what each label means and what action users should take; they do not establish that these proposed labels were deployed. (low confidence) — https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/discussions/5622
- [statement] GOV.UK contribution guidance separates proposal review for usefulness and uniqueness from implementation review for usability, consistency and versatility. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08) — https://design-system.service.gov.uk/community/contribution-criteria/
- [statement] The DTCG Format Module 2025.10 is a stable Community Group specification, explicitly neither a W3C Standard nor on the W3C Standards Track. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/
- [statement] In the DTCG format, a token type may be explicit or derived from a referenced token or the closest typed parent group; an undeterminable type is invalid, and tools must not guess it from the value. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/
- [statement] Aliases let semantic names reference underlying tokens. Contentful and Aha! illustrate keeping usage-oriented names stable while changing the primitive values selected for a theme. (high confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems · also: https://www.contentful.com/blog/design-token-system/, https://www.aha.io/engineering/articles/design-tokens-the-building-blocks-of-a-design-system
- [statement] The resolver explicitly covers light, dark and high-contrast color modes, sizing contexts, and accessibility contexts such as reduced motion; it addresses repeated token values across combinations of contexts. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/
- [statement] In the DTCG resolver, sets provide token sources and modifiers conditionally select sources through named contexts. Later sources override earlier occurrences, and the resolution order determines the final tokens. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/
